STATEMENT OF INTEREST1
Amici Curiae  Dr. Ashlee Jaffe, Barbara Medina,
Elizabeth Turnipseed, Joseph and Sheila Gutman,
Katie Woodall, Lauren Bennett, Marisa Marano, Geena
Springmann, and Peter Straus are ten survivors of two
of the deadliest mass shootings in U.S. history.  Ashlee,
Elizabeth, Joe, Sheila, Barbara, and Lauren survived the
mass shooting in Highland Park, Illinois, on July 4, 2022,
at an Independence Day parade.  Peter lost his father
in the shooting.  Katie, Geena, and Marisa survived the
Route 91 Harvest festival mass shooting on October 1,
2017, in Las Vegas, Nevada.
The shooter at the Highland Park parade fired 83
shots from an assault rifle, wounding 50 and killing seven
people in seconds.  At the Las Vegas shooting, the shooter
used over a dozen assault rifles to fire over 1,000 rounds at
concert attendees, wounding 489 and killing 58 in minutes.
Amici are all too familiar with the unique danger and
lethality of assault rifles.  The wide availability of these
military-style weapons has caused their trauma and that
of all Americans affected by a mass shooting or otherwise
injured by an assault rifle.  Amici  therefore have a
vital interest in ensuring the Constitution is correctly
interpreted to allow the enactment of reasonable gun
violence prevention laws.
1. All parties consented to the filing of this brief, and no party
or counsel for a party authored it in whole or in part.  No party,
counsel for a party, or person other than Amici Curiae or counsel
made any monetary contribution intended to fund its preparation
or submission.

2
Amici come before this Court to give voice to the
millions of Americans affected by the epidemic of mass
shootings made worse by the availability of assault rifles,
and to the many others who have been murdered and
silenced.
INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Assault rifles belong in war zones, not in the hands
of a civilian unloading into a small-town Independence
Day parade.  Assault rifles do not belong in the hands of a
civilian raining down bullets on thousands of unsuspecting
concertgoers.  Assault rifles do not belong in civilian hands
at a school, office building, place of worship, or shopping
center.  Assault rifles do not belong in civilian hands.
These weapons are designed and used to cause
as much harm to as many people as possible.  Their
effectiveness in causing mass casualties, compared with
other firearms, is why shooters favor them.
In McDonald v. City of Chicago, this Court promised
its ruling “by no means eliminates” localities’ ability “to
devise solutions to social problems that suit local needs
and values.”  561 U.S. 742, 785 (2010).  That pledge inspired
sustained engagement by the public and lawmakers to
enact effective gun laws.  This democratic feat should not
be snatched from Americans by a ruling limiting state and
local governments’ ability to enact life-saving gun laws.
This brief presents the voices of ten Americans
harmed by a mass shooting involving an assault rifle.  They
are a medical doctor who treated victims of gun violence

3
but needed the same treatment when shot at the Highland
Park parade; a young mother shot in the hip, bleeding
and unable to reach her daughter’s upended stroller at
the same shooting; and an older sister forced to abandon
friends and a bleeding woman to protect her little sister
at the Route 91 Harvest festival shooting.
For these survivors and the seven others who
volunteered their stories, restricting the availability of
assault rifles is not just a societal but a personal matter.
ARGUMENT
I.  THE REGULATION OF ASSAULT RIFLES IS
AN ISSUE OF CRITICAL IMPORTANCE TO
AMERICAN SURVIVORS OF MASS SHOOTINGS.
Mass shootings are a pressing form of American
gun violence exacerbated by the availability of assault
weapons.  One in every 15 Americans has been present
at a mass shooting at some point in their lifetime, and 2.2
percent have been injured in at least one. 2  There have
been nearly 5,000 mass shootings nationwide since 2015,
averaging 621 annually since 2020. 3  In 2025 alone, there
were 407 mass shootings, or 1.1 per day. 4
2. David C. Pyrooz et al., Direct exposure to mass shootings
among US adults , 8 JAMA Network Open 3, 6 (Mar. 7, 2025).
3. Gun Violence Archive, https://www.gunviolencearchive.
org/ (last visited Oct. 27, 2026).
4. Id.

4
Mass shootings are “an alarming public health crisis.”5
They are associated with high rates of mortality and
morbidity,6 and have far-reaching impacts on survivors and
communities.7  “Survivors of mass shootings are additional
victims.”8  They are at increased risk of mental health
issues and report persistent sadness, fear, helplessness,
and an eroded sense of safety, as well as symptoms of
depression and anxiety. 9  In communities where a mass
shooting occurred, five to ten percent of people (excluding
primary victims) suffer from posttraumatic stress
disorder (PTSD).10
Nearly all of the deadliest mass shootings in America
over the past decade involved an assault rifle. 11  The use
of assault rifles in mass shootings has increased from
19 percent in the 1990s and 2000s to 34 percent in the
2010s and 59 percent in the 2020s. 12  These aggressively

5
marketed weapons are favored by mass shooters because
of their effectiveness in achieving mass casualties while
fending off police. 13
Assault rifles turn havens into war zones: schools,
places of worship, shopping centers, entertainment venues,
restaurants, and workplaces. 14  American schoolchildren
must participate in active shooter drills in case a shooter
targets their school.
Amici share their stories here to acquaint the Court
with the terror assault rifles have inflicted on Americans,
particularly survivors of mass shootings.  Their accounts
represent the voices of survivors across America who,
suffering from the trauma caused by assault rifles and
daily mass shootings, have, through their lawmakers,
enacted laws that make their communities safer and
restore trust in the security of their homes, schools, places
of worship, and public events.
Highland Park Parade Mass Shooting
July 4, 2022, began with joy and excitement in
suburban Highland Park, Illinois.  Children adorned their
bikes and tricycles in red, white, and blue.  Parents packed
snacks and American flags and secured their babies in
strollers.  Neighbors shouted, “Happy Fourth,” as they
headed to the annual Highland Park Independence Day
Parade.  This was the first parade after a two-year pause
due to COVID-19.
13. Id.
14. Id.

6
As hundreds of families unfolded their lawn chairs and
set up camp along the parade route, a 21-year-old shooter
was perched on a rooftop overlooking them.  He held a
high-powered assault rifle and three 30-round magazines.
Fifteen minutes into the parade, he opened fire on the
spectating families.  Chaos ensued.  More than 50 people,
ranging in age from eight to 85, were wounded, and seven
were killed.  The shooter later stated he did not want to
injure people; he wanted to kill.
Liz, Ashlee, Sheila, Joe, Barbara, and Lauren attended
the parade and were wounded or had a family member
wounded.  Peter, thousands of miles away that day, lost
his father.  They shared their accounts in interviews.
A.  Liz Turnipseed
Liz hails from Philadelphia.  On July 4, 2022, she and
her husband Ian dressed their three-year-old daughter
Sonia in red, white, and blue for the parade, which Liz
had attended as a child.  They raved about the parade
to Sonia, promising floats and a band.  With any luck, it
would be the first and last Fourth of July Sonia spent as
an only child—Liz was scheduled for an embryo transfer
in early August.
On their way, Sonia could see that, like her, everyone
was wearing red, white, and blue.  “There were just so
many children,” Liz recalls.  “They had decorated their
bikes and tricycles with red, white, and blue streamers
so they could ride in the parade.”  The family was late but
found an open spot in front of Walker Brothers, the local
pancake house.  They sat directly across from the rooftop
where the shooter was waiting.

7
Ian stood behind Liz, and Sonia watched from her
stroller.  Women on horseback led the parade, followed by
first responders, fire truck drivers, and EMTs with their
families.  They gathered at the end of the parade route for
a community festival while the parade continued.
Next came lawmakers, veterans, and the park district.
Camp counselors and lifeguards handed out candy and
packets of seeds to kids.  Then came the thunderous chorus
of the marching band.  The shooter held his fire.  He had
friends in the band.
But as the band passed Walker Brothers, Liz heard
a “pop-pop-pop-pop-pop.”  She thought someone had lit
fireworks.  She looked toward Sonia, felt a sharp sensation
on her hip, and fell.  A high-pitched sound rang in her ears
from the supersonic bullets whizzing overhead.  She lifted
her head and saw Sonia’s stroller flipped onto its side.  Liz
could not see her baby.  A searing pain shot through her
side.  Ian appeared and pulled her behind a crowded bike
rack.  He had Sonia, and she was alive.  Ian had flipped
Sonia’s stroller over and taken her into his arms when
the shooting began.  Liz told him to run with Sonia.  Ian
cradled Sonia like a football and ran.
Alone, bleeding, and unable to move, Liz lay behind the
bike rack as bullets rained down on the parade.  At first,
she thought it was a terrorist attack but soon realized it
was a mass shooting.  The bullets came in waves: a brief
pause, then more rapid fire.  She watched bullets and
shrapnel ricochet off the ground among the abandoned
flags and bikes.  It became quiet again.  Those who
remained were wounded or dead.  To her left, Liz saw the
feet of a lifeless couple she later learned were Kevin and

8
Irina McCarthy.  Their two-year-old boy wandered in the
street through the dead and dying.
Ian handed Sonia to a stranger and ran back to Liz.
The woman yelled out her name, but Ian did not catch it.
Liz made him go back to find out who had their daughter.
Finally, the Lake County Sheriff reached Liz and applied
pressure to her leg.  As the Sheriff treated her, Liz saw
paramedics giving chest compressions to a man she later
learned was 88-year-old Stephen Straus.  On the street
behind Liz was an eight-year-old boy who was shot in the
back with a bullet that exited his chest, damaging his
aorta, liver, esophagus, and spinal cord, and permanently
paralyzing him from the waist down.
Liz was taken to Lake Forest Hospital.  She was
discharged after three days, only to return with
unexplained bleeding.  The bullet had left a 14 cm hole
in her leg that would not close—a hematoma filled with
blood and dead tissue.  For 30 days, she was connected to
a vacuum-assisted wound-closure device to remove fluid
and accelerate her healing.  The hematoma has shrunk,
but Liz lives with chronic pain.  She has bullet fragments
in her leg, hip, and buttocks and therefore cannot get an
MRI.  Liz cannot sit at her desk for long.  For months after
the shooting, she could not care for Sonia.  When the day
came that Liz could again stand at the counter and cook
dinner, she wept.
Liz suffers from PTSD, depression, and anxiety, and is
hypervigilant: “Any stress can trigger nightmares.”  She
is in regular cognitive behavioral therapy.  She and Ian do
not go to Chicago Cubs games anymore.  Sonia refers to
what happened as the “loud noise machine and the glass

9
balls,” and she has trouble attending birthday parties or
gym class; the sounds of children screaming and running
around can be triggering.
Liz did not make it to her follow-up IVF appointment.
The embryo transfer scheduled for August never
happened.  The extensive nerve damage has made it
impossible for Liz to have another child.
B.  Dr. Ashlee Jaffe
“I am a survivor,” Dr. Ashlee Jaffe whispered to
herself as she waited alone to deliver a speech against gun
violence in 2024.  Ashlee never thought she would be on
the other side of gun violence.  She is a doctor specializing
in pediatric rehabilitation, regularly treating patients
with firearms-related injuries.  Her work focuses on the
long-lasting impact of being shot by a single bullet.  That
work was clinical, until July 4, 2022.
Born and raised in the Highland Park area, Ashlee
returned on Independence Day weekend to celebrate the
holiday and her father’s birthday.  Ashlee, her husband,
and their five-year-old son met friends for breakfast at
Walker Brothers before the parade.  After breakfast, they
stepped outside to watch the parade.  Ashlee claimed a
bench outside the pancake house.  She sat down with her
friend’s two-year-old son on her lap, her own son at her
side, and her friend’s mother and two friends gathered
around.  Ashlee had “no idea that someone had climbed
on top of the building across the street.”
As she heard a pop-pop-pop, Ashlee felt a sudden
pain in her hand.  She was confused.  She looked to see

10
where the sound originated as her brain caught up and
registered that shots were coming.  “It felt like a dream
where you’re trying to scream but can’t.”  She looked down
and saw blood.  Then, more shots.  Ashlee knew she had
been hit but hesitated, afraid of crying wolf and causing a
stampede: “It took time for people to stop focusing on the
parade and realize it was a war zone developing around
them.”
More shots.  Now there was no doubt.  Ashlee
screamed that she was hit, threw her friend’s son to the
ground, and yelled for someone to take him, not knowing
whether he had also been shot.  It was as if she were on a
battlefield, making split-second decisions to survive.  “I did
not know what the right thing to do was.”  Ashlee’s watch
had been shot off her wrist.  She saw her son walking into
the street to retrieve it.  She grabbed him, pulled him
under the bench, and wrapped her body around him.  She
saw that her husband had grabbed her friend’s son.  She
saw people lying dead on the ground.  She saw paramedics
performing chest compressions on Jacki Sundheim, a
preschool teacher who later died.  A man ran across the
street with bullet wounds in his chest.  Ashlee wanted to
help but knew the battlefield rule: victims must first help
themselves.  The bullets came in volleys—83 shots in all,
from three magazines.  It was “terrifying.”
Things became quiet, but it was not clear whether
the shooting had stopped.  Ashlee handed her husband
her wedding ring so it would not be cut off in surgery.  A
SWAT officer told them to evacuate the area as the scene
was not secure.  Ashlee’s husband took their son and her
friend’s son into a nearby shop.  Her friend appeared out

11
of nowhere and rushed Ashlee to Highland Park Hospital,
where Ashlee had been born.
The hospital waiting room was filled with wounded
people.  Ashlee, in doctor mode, handed washcloths to the
bleeding to use on their wounds.  “Code blue, code blue”
sounded over the loudspeakers, and she knew someone
was at risk of death.  Ambulances and wounded people
kept coming.  Families were kept out to make space for
the wounded, but her friend’s mother was allowed inside to
accompany Ashlee.  A man in the waiting room remarked
that he had done two tours in Vietnam and had never been
shot—until that day.
Eventually Ashlee’s husband transported her to the
less busy Lutheran General Hospital.  There, the shooting
played on a loop on the TV screens.  Only then did Ashlee
notice the additional wound on her elbow.  Ashlee’s hand is
permanently damaged.  She has lost strength in her grip,
and her injured hand cannot sense heat.  She would not
dare take a hot lasagna out of the oven; she might burn
without knowing it.
Ashlee also struggles mentally.  She attended a
baseball game once but stayed near an elevator in the back
the entire game.  The same trauma grips her son, who
wanted to write an essay in third grade arguing that only
the military should have big guns.  Through her advocacy,
Ashlee hopes the Highland Park shooting is the last one
her son experiences.

12
C.  Peter Straus
Peter, who lives in San Francisco, grew up in Highland
Park.  His father, Stephen Straus, died there in the July
4th shooting.  Stephen had been a sharpshooter in the
army during peacetime, so Peter grew up around guns.
Peter still owns guns, for target shooting, a pastime
from his childhood.  Assault rifles, he says, “are made for
destroying, killing, and maiming, not protecting.”
The Highland Park Independence Day parade was a
Straus family tradition—Peter remembers attending in
1976.  Peter’s mother was disabled, so Stephen went alone.
Stephen stood in front of Walker Brothers, across from
the roof where the shooter was positioned.  The shooter
later told police that he targeted older adults like Stephen
and wanted to kill them, aiming from the waist up.  He
shot Stephen multiple times.
A friend texted Peter that there was gunfire at the
parade.  Peter tried to reach his father, but his calls failed
each time.  Then his brother called.  “Dad’s dead.”  Peter
could not process what he heard.  He knew his brother
wouldn’t joke; he just didn’t want it to be true.  “My dad
was gone, I’d never be able to say goodbye, or thank you,
or I love you.  Everything changed in an instant.”
Peter’s mother, who had relied on Stephen to care for
her, moved into assisted living six months later and carries
on alone.  Stephen’s death left a void for Peter’s brother and
his children, who lived nearby and had seen Stephen the
night before.  Stephen was “a warm, gentle, thoughtful and
kind man.”  He had worked as a stockbroker in downtown
Chicago most of his life.  He was still working and showed

13
no signs of slowing down, going on walks and riding his
bike regularly.
“I have shot a semi-automatic assault rifle, but I can’t
for the life of me understand why a civilian would own such
a thing, because it’s clearly only a weapon of war if you’ve
shot one,” Peter said.  “It’s not a hunting gun.  It should
be owned only by military or law enforcement.”
D.  Sheila and Joe Gutman
On July 4, 2022, a single bullet from the shooter’s
assault rifle shattered and shredded Sheila’s foot.  Joe,
her husband, was with her.
Sheila and Joe attended the parade with family,
including their three adult sons, their sons’ wives, and
their grandchildren.  They watched from lawn chairs just
east of Walker Brothers.  One grandchild, just a year old,
sat in a stroller.  When the gunshots started, Sheila did not
think much of it.  Joe thought it was a bunch of “knuckleheaded kids” setting off firecrackers.  But the sounds kept
coming, and then bodies began falling.  Chaos erupted as
people scrambled for cover.  Sheila remembers the bullets
coming fast after each brief pause.  An elderly woman was
bleeding in front of her.  Sheila tried to run but couldn’t.
Her foot was heavy, and lifting it brought searing pain.
Someone grabbed the baby from the stroller, and the
family ran for cover.  When Joe saw that Sheila wasn’t
moving, he and one of their sons carried her.  Shop owners,
fearing they might be the shooters, would not let them in.
Instead, the family found a hallway in a U-shaped corridor
of shops and offices.

14
Joe stepped back outside when the shooting stopped.
“I t  w as  a  w ar  z o n e , ”  h e  r e call s .   Tw o  SW A T  o ffi c e rs
sprinted past him with guns drawn.  Along the parade
route, medics were covering the dead.  People were
running aimlessly, searching for family or safety.  Many
of the wounded and dead lay near Walker Brothers,
where his family had been sitting.  It was the “hot zone”:
the shooter was perched directly across from the area,
so most of his bullets landed there.  Everyone within five
feet of them was shot, killed, or knew someone who was.
The woman sitting next to them was shot in the pelvis.  A
girl who sat across from them was hit in the foot—she is
the one who found Aiden McCarthy, the wandering twoyear-old whose parents, Kevin and Irina, had been killed.
Sheila’s foot created a pool of blood in the hallway
where her family hid.  The family took her to Lake
Forest Hospital, where a family friend happened to be a
surgeon.  He brought in a specialist, and they operated
on Sheila immediately.  Sheila’s wounds were unlike
anything civilian trauma centers experience.  Wounds
like hers are found among soldiers at war, not here.  The
bullet “eviscerated” her foot.  The surgeons sought advice
from multiple trauma centers around the country.  They
attached two rounds of flap grafts to replace the missing
tissue and skin.  They considered amputating her foot.
“Just let me die,” she cried.  Despite keeping her foot,
Sheila will never be the same.
Her recovery has been long and painful: 17 surgeries,
45 days hospitalized (six in intensive care), and 22 sessions
in a hyperbaric chamber.  Sheila has been in physical
therapy ever since the shooting.  She could not walk for

15
over a year, even after regaining mobility.  Her physical
challenges continue.
The trauma runs deep.  Every family member who
attended the parade has been affected.  “The aftermath
is brutal,” Sheila says.  “Someone can heal from physical
harm, but not isolation and dependency.”  Not a day goes
by when she does not suffer from the incident.  She believes
it is her responsibility to teach others about the terror of
assault rifles and the trauma of mass shootings.  Joe puts it
plainly: “[I]f it was not a military grade style assault rifle,
maybe they would have gotten off 13 shots instead of 83.”
E.  Barbara Medina
Barbara, a resident of Highland Park, participated in
the 2022 parade with her father and two children, then
ages seven and 12, along with a friend and the friend’s
children.
Barbara and her family did not witness the carnage
that day.  As they approached a corner to turn onto Central
Avenue, the shots rang out, and hundreds of people
swarmed them, fleeing.  She was carrying one side of a
large banner and, when she realized there was a shooting,
told the woman on the other side to drop it and run.
Barbara could not see her children or father, who
were also marching in the parade, handing out candy
and carrying a float.  As she ran to find them, she saw
her daughter on her scooter about to be trampled by the
stampeding crowd as everyone funneled down an alleyway.
Barbara reached down to lift her seven-year-old off her
scooter so she wouldn’t get run over, tripped over the

16
scooter, and broke her arm.  “I tend to sugarcoat it, but
it was terrifying.  I watched my arm going in the wrong
direction as I hit the ground, was run over by a guy on a
bike and had to reset my own arm,” she says.  Knowing
her injury would prevent her from running quickly, she
planned to hide under a car with her daughter, but at the
last moment, a woman opened a courtyard door to her
townhouse complex and took them into her home.  By then,
everyone had scattered.  Barbara did not know where her
son and father were or if they were in danger.  It would
be four or five hours before everyone found each other.
Highland Park Hospital was overflowing, so Barbara
had a friend drive her to Skokie Hospital to treat her
broken elbow once they could leave their shelter.  Though
she had two surgeries to replace the shattered radial head,
she still cannot fully straighten her arm, experiences
nerve pain, and suffers from continued medical issues
related to a blood disorder triggered by the injury.
The family tries not to let the memory control, but
they suffer from anxiety and PTSD.  At large events, they
look for the exits first and avoid anywhere they might
be trapped.  Fear precedes fun.  Her son has developed
tics that flare up with loud noises or large crowds.   When
Barbara leaves their home, he asks, “What if there is a
shooting and you die this time?”
F.  Lauren Bennett
Lauren is a longtime Highland Park resident.  Her
sons were born there.  She and her husband loved the
parade; he had been going since he was a toddler.  On July
4, 2022, they arrived early, at 8:30 a.m., and saved seats

17
near Walker Brothers.  They had never sat there before
but wanted a good spot for the boys to grab candy from
the camp counselors and lifeguards.
Minutes into the parade, just after the band had
passed, Lauren heard a noise: “It sounded like those snaps
that kids play with.”  She felt a shock on her hip and looked
down.  There was blood all over.  She knew she had been
shot.  No one else had noticed.  The parade was proceeding,
and everyone was watching.  But when Lauren screamed
that they were being shot at, everyone started running.
The scene replays in Lauren’s mind like a movie: “It was
like a hailstorm of concrete in every direction and chaos
started.  I thought it was a militia coming after us because
of all the bullets.  I never would have thought it was one
person with a gun.”
As Lauren got up to run, she felt a shock in her back;
she had been shot again.  She could not see her children but
knew she had to find safety, so she dove into a nearby bush.
“In the bushes, I looked at myself completely covered in
blood, just soaked.”  Somewhere, her husband was running
with their children while shouting for people to flee.
She emerged from the bushes.  “I started running
and I was just dripping with blood.  I was just running for
safety.  I knew I needed a doctor.”  Her husband caught
up with her in their car.  Other paradegoers surrounded
the car and begged for a ride, but they could not take
them.  Her husband drove over lawns and around crowds
of panicked people.  Her children were in the back seat
crying; they had seen their mom’s bloody hip.  She thought
she might die.

18
They were the first to arrive at the hospital.  The
doctors and nurses looked puzzled; they didn’t know yet.
Then, ambulances swarmed the emergency room and
chaos ensued.  Lauren heard children crying and the
recitation of last rites.  Doctors found two holes in her
back where she had been shot.  The bullets had barely
missed her heart and lungs.  They stitched her up, and the
shrapnel worked its way out over time.  Lauren’s husband
took their sons home and put on a movie, trying to shield
them from what was happening.
Images of the shooting repeat in Lauren’s mind daily.
“It’s a part of me.  It’s in me.  I’m always thinking of it
and I’m always scared.  If this can happen to us in this
nice safe community, then it could happen anywhere at
any time.”  Lauren tries to stay strong for her boys.  For
a long time, her older son brought a bulletproof vest to
school as a safety tool, like a blanket.  Her youngest stays
with the principal when they have mass shooting drills.
“It makes me mad.  My kids.  They have their whole lives
ahead of them and this will be with them forever, for their
whole lives.”
The Fourth of July is somber now.  They cannot be
around sudden loud noises.  They no longer go to Disney
World every year.  They are constantly looking over their
shoulders, for places to run or hide.  “It’s really hard to
live.  We do the best we can.  It’s one day at a time.”
Knowing there was only one shooter makes Lauren
even angrier: “In the moments that it happened, my mind
was thinking there is an army coming after us.  I never
knew a lot about these guns.  I never thought about it.
But when we were in the hospital and learned there was

19
one shooter they were looking for, I was shocked.  In the
hospital they were bringing in bloody body after bloody
body.  I would never have thought that could happen with
one person and one gun.”
Route 91 Harvest Festival Mass Shooting
The Route 91 Harvest country music festival sold out
months before opening on September 29, 2017.  Held at
Las Vegas Village, across from the Mandalay Bay Hotel,
it drew more than 40,000 fans to see music stars like
Jason Aldean, Eric Church, and Sam Hunt.  Aldean was
scheduled to close the festival with a late-night set on
October 1.  Tens of thousands of concertgoers crowded
the field when he took the stage.
As fans listened to Aldean’s performance, a 64-yearold businessman on the 32 nd floor of the Mandalay Bay
Hotel loaded up 14 semiautomatic assault rifles, ten
handguns, bump stocks, and numerous high-capacity
magazines capable of holding up to 100 rounds each.  From
there, he looked straight down on the crowd, packed into
the middle of the field.  The shooter had cased hotel rooms
in the area a week earlier and settled on this one.
At 10:05 p.m., he began shooting into the crowd.
In just ten minutes, he fired more than 1,000 rounds,
wounding over 800 concertgoers and killing 58.  Katie,
Marisa, and Geena were in the crowd.
G.  Katie Woodall
Katie was a preschool teacher, mom, and wife.  She
attended the concert with her husband Wayne and two

20
other couples.  They moved closer to the stage to get the
best view of Jason Aldean’s performance.  The concert
lights silhouetted them against the darkness.
Katie was singing and dancing with her husband and
friends when she thought she heard fireworks.  Then their
husbands shouted in unison that someone was shooting,
and they hit the ground.  They got up to run, but Katie
was struggling.  Wayne asked if she had been shot; she
did not know.
Out of nowhere, a concert attendee who identified
himself as a former military medic ran over to help.  He
saw that Katie had been shot, applied compression, and
noted with concern that there appeared to be no exit
wounds.  He explained that they could not stay where
they were because they were illuminated by the concert
lights, making them easier targets for the gunman and
his powerful weapon.  “No one is coming to get you,” the
medic said.
Drawing on his military experience, and aware that
the shooter was using an assault weapon, he explained that
the shooter would have to pause briefly to reload and that
this would be their moment to run.  Together they moved
over shards of glass and overturned tables toward a dark
area so he could treat her further.  As they crawled, blood
splattered on Katie’s face, and she wondered with horror
whether Wayne had been hit.  But when she turned, she
saw that a woman next to her had been shot in the neck.
The medic told them to continue ahead on their own; the
woman needed aid even more urgently.

21
The gunfire briefly paused, and Katie and Wayne
bolted for safety.  Katie saw people frantically loading
a friend’s bullet-riddled body into a wheelbarrow and
rushing toward the exit.  She saw men who had attempted
to shield their wives from bullets now lying dead on the
concert field.  The screams of people realizing a loved one
had died still ring in her ears.  As she and Wayne ran,
Katie’s pain worsened.  She told Wayne, “I can’t do this
anymore; you just need to tell the boys that I love them.”
Wayne refused, “I will not do that.  You are going to tell
the boys that you love them.  You are not going to give up
. . . this is not going to be the end of our story.  You are
not going to die here.”
Katie and Wayne eventually made it to an ambulance,
which was crammed with victims.  At the hospital, Katie
underwent surgery.  Her colon was damaged, and the
bullet was lodged in her oblique muscles.  The doctors
had manipulated and moved around her organs, bruising
them and causing her to feel like her insides had been
beaten with a baseball bat for years after the surgery.
She spent six days in the hospital and three months in
recovery.  The bullet remains inside, a painful reminder.
Katie has been diagnosed with PTSD and continues to
struggle.  Death is more salient in her mind now.  Before
leaving for a vacation, she replays in her head the right
words to let her kids know their importance and the joy
they have brought to her life, in case she is killed.
Still, Katie finds strength to advocate for survivors
of mass shootings and against assault rifles by sharing
her story: “We were thrust into a kind of horror we never
could have imagined existed.  Because our country allows
people to purchase assault rifles my husband and I found

22
ourselves in a combat zone in which innocent civilians
who had no military training and no means to defend
themselves were being gunned down.”
H.  Marisa Marano and Geena Springmann
Marisa and Geena are sisters and clinical social
workers who treat traumatized individuals.  The sisters
attended the concert together.  For Marisa, it was one of
those rare nights out for a parent with a young child.  They
met Geena’s friends on the concert grounds.
A few minutes after Jason Aldean began his
performance, they heard shots.  Like many, they initially
thought they heard fireworks.  But when someone yelled
“get down,” they hit the deck.  Marisa wrapped her body
around Geena to shield her from the bullets.  “The gunfire
came in waves,” Geena remembered.  There would be a
“burst of gunfire,” and then a lull.  The bullets came in
rapid succession, “pop-pop-pop-pop-pop.”  They sprinted
from the scene after five minutes, running past a woman
in a white shirt covered in blood.  They had to protect
themselves and each other.  They became separated from
their friends.  “People were falling left and right, and you
did not know where the shots were coming from.”
Geena left behind her purse, wallet, and keys.  While
fleeing, she called her mother but could not reach her.
Her mother responded with a text asking why Geena had
called.  Geena replied, “shooting.”  Her mother replied in
horror, “what’s going on, by you?”  She let her mother know
that it was at the festival and added, “We are running I
love you.”  Her mother asked if they were at the MGM and
said they should stay there because the shooter wouldn’t

23
come inside.  She told Geena that their father was coming,
so they should tell him their location. Geena texted back,
“Mom not now lots of bodies.”  She tried the police, but
the call could not go through.  She texted her boyfriend
(now husband) and his family to let them know as well.
The sisters sought shelter at the MGM hotel, but the
doors were locked.  After a restaurant manager opened
a side door, they broke down.  The hotel patrons and
staff were confused, unaware of the shooting, telling the
sisters to “calm down.”  Finally, their father found them
and drove them home.  The ride was silent as the scene
replayed in their minds.  At home, their mother was
hysterical.  Early news reports indicated perhaps six or
seven deaths, but Geena knew dozens were injured or
dead.  They were shocked to learn the shooting had lasted
ten minutes because “it felt like hours, and the bullets
just kept coming.”
Marisa and Geena carry hidden scars.  Both have
PTSD and are now hypervigilant about their surroundings.
Geena avoids crowded events.  As a mother, she hopes her
child never experiences a mass shooting.  Whenever there
is a school shooting, she is reminded of her own fear.  At
a football game where a gun was fired to start the game,
she instantly fell to the ground in a fetal position.  She left
a movie theater in the middle of the film when she saw a
man with a suspicious bag.
Marisa has not attended another outdoor concert since
that night.  She looks for the exit when she attends events
and struggles to trust people.  She once left a grocery store
early when she noticed a person carrying a firearm.  She
and her husband have enrolled their children in private

24
schools with security.  They are gun owners, but Marisa
does not believe anyone should own an assault rifle.  She
knows firsthand that “these weapons are designed to kill
as many people as possible.”
II.  THE CHALLENGED ASSAULT WEAPON
BANS REFLECT FOUNDING-ERA LAWS THAT
PROTECTED AGAINST THE EXACT “TERROR”
EXPERIENCED BY THESE VICTIMS OF MASS

AND UNUSUAL WEAPONS.
Amici’s experiences and injuries underscore the unique
lethality of AR-15s and similar semiautomatic assault
rifles.  The assault rifle is a Goldilocks of death because
it combines the most lethal features of more traditional
categories of military small arms into one deadly package.
For example, assault rifles combine the accuracy and
flesh-tearing kinetic energy of a rifle cartridge, the rate
of fire and smoothness of a semiautomatic firearm, and
the capacity and maneuverability of a submachine gun.
Proponents of these weapons do not dispute this; they
celebrate it.  The government writes that “AR-15s are
highly useful for self-defense, both in their capacity for
deterrence and in their lethality.”  U.S. Br. 23.  But assault
rifles are not designed for self-defense; they are designed
for military assaults.  And their lethality is not a cause
for celebration.

A.  The Second Amendment Permits State and
Local Governments to Regulate Assault Rifles
As They Are Uniquely Dangerous Weapons
That Terrorize Americans
This Court has explained that “[f]rom Blackstone
through the 19th-century cases, commentators and courts
routinely explained that the right [to keep and bear arms]
was not a right to keep and carry any weapon whatsoever
in any manner whatsoever and for whatever purpose.”
Heller, 554 U.S. at 626.  The Court has recognized the gun
violence problem in America and stated the Constitution
leaves governments “a variety of tools for combating that
problem,” including regulation.  Id. at 636.
As the Connecticut Respondents explain, American
history shows governments can prohibit unusually
dangerous weapons.  See Br. for Conn. Resp. 9-37; see
also Heller , 554 U.S. at 626-627.  This centuries-long
historical tradition includes Founding-era laws prohibiting
the common-law offense of “riding or going armed, with
dangerous or unusual weapons . . . by terrifying the
good people of the land.”  4 Commentaries on the Laws
of England 11 (1765-1769) (Blackstone).  This reflects the
purpose of the laws enacted by Connecticut and Cook
County.  These local laws are designed to prevent another
mass shooter from coming armed with an assault rifle,
a dangerous and unusual weapon, into a public place or
event to the terror of people such as Amici.
Survivors of mass shootings understand the value of
public debate and action through the democratic process,
especially on this issue.  They have spoken out against gun
violence and advocated for safer gun laws.  Their voices

31
cannot be fully heard if their governments cannot act on
an issue that has caused them significant trauma.  This
Court should keep its promise to them and the millions of
other Americans affected by mass gun violence daily that
“state and local experimentation with reasonable firearm
regulations will continue under the Second Amendment.”
McDonald, 561 U.S. at 785 (citation and brackets omitted).
State and local governments and their citizens must be
granted room to shape policy around this issue, as it
involves a stark tradeoff with the right of Americans to
stay alive, safe, and unbroken.
CONCLUSION
Amici  urge the Court to uphold the State of
Connecticut and Cook County’s assault rifle restrictions,
so that no more mass shooters go armed with this
dangerous weapon to the terror of more Americans.
